name: First Repeated Barcode
background: Barcodes arrive one at a time and each is checked against everything seen so far. The answer is the value of the first barcode that turns out to be a repeat, meaning it is reported at its SECOND appearance, not its first. Only the value is printed, not its position.
task: Read N barcodes in arrival order and print the value of the first barcode that repeats an earlier one, or -1 if no barcode repeats.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Duplicate Email Position
background: Addresses are scanned left to right and each is checked against the ones already seen. The answer is the position of the first address that repeats an earlier entry, counted from 1. Since positions start at 1, the value 0 is free to mean 'no duplicates at all'.
task: Read N email addresses and print the 1-based index of the first address that duplicates an earlier entry, or 0 if all addresses are unique.

addresses: 1-30 characters, no spaces, case-sensitive

name: Repeated Sensor Reading
background: Sensor IDs are read in order and each is checked against everything seen before it. Positions start at 0 here, so the very first reading sits at position 0. If every reading is unique the word OK is printed instead of a position.
task: Read N sensor IDs and print the earliest 0-based position at which an ID has already been seen before, or OK if every reading is unique.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

task: Read N card codes in deal order and print the code whose second occurrence happens earliest, or NONE if every card is unique.

name: Two Values Summing to Target
background: Two DIFFERENT positions must be chosen, though the values sitting there may happen to be equal. When several pairs work, the answer is pinned down by taking the smallest first index, and among those the smallest second index.
task: Read N integers and a target T. Print the 1-based indices i and j (with i < j) of a pair whose values sum to T, choosing the smallest i and then the smallest j. Print '-1 -1' if no pair exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Two Values with a Given Difference
background: Orientation matters here: the value at the first index minus the value at the second must equal K, so swapping the two indices generally gives a different result. The two indices must differ, though the same element can never be used twice. Ties are settled by the smallest first index, then the smallest second.
task: Read N integers and a value K. Print the 1-based indices i and j (i not equal to j) such that a[i] - a[j] = K, choosing the smallest i and then the smallest j. Print NONE if no such pair exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Two Values with a Given XOR
background: XOR compares two numbers bit by bit and keeps a 1 wherever exactly one of them had a 1. A useful consequence is that any number XORed with itself gives 0, so a repeated value forms a pair whose XOR is 0. Ties are settled by the smallest first index, then the smallest second.
task: Read N non-negative integers and a target X. Print the 1-based indices i and j (with i < j) of a pair whose XOR equals X, choosing the smallest i and then the smallest j. Print '-1 -1' if no such pair exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N, X (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.

name: Two Weights Filling the Capacity
background: Two different items must be chosen, even if two items happen to weigh the same. What gets printed is the two WEIGHTS rather than their positions. Ties are settled by taking the pair with the smallest first position, then the smallest second.
task: Read N item weights and a capacity C. Print the two weights of a pair of distinct items that sum to C, taken from the pair with the smallest first index then smallest second index, in that index order. Print IMPOSSIBLE if no such pair exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N, C (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Complement Index for Everyone
background: Every position gets its own answer: some other position whose value completes the sum S. An element may never be paired with itself, though it can pair with a different element holding an identical value. Where several partners work, the earliest one is chosen, and -1 marks positions with no partner at all.
task: Read N integers and a target S. For each position i print an index j (1-based, j not equal to i) such that a[i] + a[j] = S, choosing the smallest such j, or -1 if no partner exists. Print the N answers in order.
input_format:
Line 1: N, S (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: IDs Above a Frequency Bar
background: Every distinct ID is counted across the whole list first, then judged against the threshold. 'At least T' includes exactly T, so an ID seen precisely T times qualifies. Each qualifying ID is reported once regardless of how often it occurred.
task: Read N integer IDs and a threshold T. Print every distinct ID occurring at least T times, in increasing order. If none qualify, print an empty line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Same Magnitudes
background: A multiset cares about which values are present AND how many times each occurs, but not about their order. Here every value is first replaced by its absolute value, so -3 and 3 become indistinguishable. The two collections match only if every magnitude appears the same number of times in both, which also requires equal lengths.
task: Read two integer arrays A and B. Replacing every element by its absolute value, print YES if the two arrays then contain exactly the same multiset of values, otherwise NO.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers (array A).
Line 3: M.
Line 4: M space-separated integers (array B).

name: Two Coins Summing to Target
background: Because the coin values are already sorted, two pointers starting at the ends can walk toward each other: if the current sum is too small the left pointer moves right, and if too large the right pointer moves left. Ties are settled by the smallest first index, then the smallest second.

name: Two Timestamps a Fixed Gap Apart
background: The list is already nondecreasing, so a later index never holds a smaller timestamp. The search wants a pair whose later value exceeds the earlier one by exactly D; note that D may be 0, which asks for two equal timestamps. Ties go to the smallest first index, then the smallest second.

name: Two Weights Closest to Target
background: No pair need hit the target exactly; the goal is the pair whose sum is nearest to it, measured as the absolute distance from T. A sum may overshoot or undershoot, and a sum 3 above T is just as good as one 3 below. Ties are settled by the smallest first index, then the smallest second.

name: Bookings Per Day
background: Each booking adds one to every day in its inclusive range. Rather than touching every day, a difference array marks a +1 where the range begins and a -1 just past where it ends, and a single running total then reveals each day's count.
task: Read N days starting at zero bookings and Q bookings, each 'l r' incrementing every day from l to r inclusive. Print the booking count for each of the N days.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Next Q lines: l and r, separated by a space.

name: Paint Thickness Per Panel
background: Each stroke adds a thickness to every panel in an inclusive range, and that amount may be negative, which thins the paint instead. A difference array records only the boundaries of each stroke, and one running total recovers every panel's final thickness. Negative results are possible.
task: Read N panels starting at zero thickness and Q strokes, each 'l r d' adding d (possibly negative) to every panel from l to r inclusive. Print the final thickness of each panel.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Next Q lines: l, r and d, separated by spaces.

name: Priciest Toll Booth
background: Each regulation adds a delta to every booth in an inclusive range, and deltas may be negative. After all regulations are applied, the booth with the highest final fee is reported; if several booths tie at that maximum, the one with the smallest index wins. Booth indices start at 1.
task: Read N toll booths starting at fee 0 and Q regulations, each 'l r delta' adding delta to every booth from l to r inclusive. Print the 1-based index of the booth with the maximum final fee (smallest index on ties) followed by that maximum fee.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Next Q lines: l, r and delta, separated by spaces.

name: Well-Covered Points
background: Each camera adds one to the coverage of every point in its inclusive range. After all cameras are installed, a point counts as well covered when its coverage is at least K, so exactly K qualifies. Points covered by no camera have coverage 0.
task: Read N points starting uncovered, Q camera ranges each 'l r', and a threshold K. Print how many of the N points end up with coverage at least K.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q, K (space-separated).
Next Q lines: l and r, separated by a space.

name: Simple Parenthesis Check
background: A stack tracks the openings that are still waiting to be closed: each '(' is pushed and each ')' pops the most recent one. Two things can go wrong: a ')' arriving when nothing is waiting, or the string ending with openings still on the stack. In the first case the offending closer is reported, in the second the earliest unmatched opener.
task: Read a string of '(' and ')'. Print YES if it is properly nested. If a closing bracket arrives with nothing to close, print its 1-based index. If the string ends with unmatched openings, print the 1-based index of the first unmatched opening.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (characters '(' and ')' only).

name: Typed Bracket Check
background: Three kinds of brackets must nest properly AND match by type, so ']' can only close '['. The stack holds openings still waiting. A closer is invalid if the stack is empty or if the top opening is the wrong type. If the string ends with openings left over, the earliest of those is reported.
task: Read a string of the six characters ( ) [ ] { }. Print VALID if the delimiters are properly nested with matching types. If a closing bracket mismatches or closes nothing, print its 1-based index. If the string ends with leftover openings, print the 1-based index of the first unmatched opening.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (characters ( ) [ ] { } only).

name: Brackets Outside Quotes
background: Anything sitting between a pair of double quotes is a quoted token, and delimiters inside it are literal text that must be ignored entirely. Only the brackets outside quotes are checked, with '(' matching ')' and '<' matching '>'. Quotes are guaranteed to come in pairs.
task: Read a string of ( ) < > and double-quote characters, where delimiters inside a quoted section are ignored. Print OK if the unquoted delimiters nest properly, otherwise print the 1-based index of the first invalid character. If openings are left over, print the index of the first unmatched opening.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (characters ( ) < > and " only).
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
double quotes always come in matched pairs

name: Brackets Outside Single Quotes
background: Text between a pair of single quotes is a quoted token whose brackets are literal and must be ignored. Only unquoted delimiters are validated, with '[' matching ']' and '<' matching '>'. Since positions start at 1, the value 0 is free to mean 'balanced'. Quotes always come in pairs.
task: Read a string of [ ] < > and single-quote characters, where delimiters inside a quoted section are ignored. Print 0 if the unquoted delimiters nest properly, otherwise print the 1-based position of the first violating character. If openings are left over, print the position of the first unmatched opening.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (characters [ ] < > and ' only).
constraints:
length of S: 1-100
single quotes always come in matched pairs

name: Full Bracket Validation
background: Brackets must close in reverse order of opening and must match by type, so '}' only closes '{'. An early closing is invalid when nothing is waiting or when the waiting opener is the wrong type. Leftover openings at the end are reported by the earliest one.
task: Read a string of the six characters ( ) [ ] { }. Print Matched if the string is balanced. If a closing is invalid, print its 1-based index. If the string finishes with unmatched openings, print the 1-based index of the first unmatched opening.
input_format: Line 1: the string S (characters ( ) [ ] { } only).

Because a removal can expose a new top, cancellations can cascade, so only same-pole magnets can survive together.

name: Fit the Most Meetings
background: Half-open meetings [s, e) let one meeting start exactly when another ends. The classic greedy rule is to always take the compatible meeting that FINISHES earliest, which leaves the most room for what follows. Ties on finish time are settled by earlier start, then smaller index.
task: Read N meeting requests as half-open intervals [s, e). Using the greedy earliest-finishing rule (ties broken by earlier start, then smaller index), select a maximum-size set of non-overlapping meetings and print their 1-based indices in the order chosen.

Next N lines: start and end, separated by a space.
constraints:

intervals satisfy start < end
times: 0-100000

background: Closed segments [s, e] include both endpoints, so a segment ending at 10 CONFLICTS with one starting at 10: they share that instant. The next segment must therefore start strictly after the previous one ends. Only the count of selected segments is reported.
task: Read N radio segments as closed intervals [s, e], where touching segments conflict. Print the maximum number of segments that can be aired on one frequency without conflict.

times: 0-100000

task: Read N tasks with decimal start and end times, treated as (s, e] so a task may start exactly when another ends. Using the greedy earliest-finishing rule (ties broken by earlier start, then smaller index), print the 1-based indices of a maximum-size selection in increasing finish order.

intervals satisfy start < end
times: 0.0-1000.0, given with one decimal place

task: Read N talk proposals as half-open intervals [s, e). Using the greedy earliest-finishing rule (ties broken by earlier start, then smaller index), print the number of talks scheduled on the first line and their 1-based indices in chronological order on the second.

times: 0-100000

task: Read N surgery appointments as closed intervals [s, e], where touching appointments overlap. Using the greedy earliest-finishing rule (ties broken by earlier start, then smaller index), print the 1-based indices of a maximum-size selection in the order chosen.

background: Because each denomination is a multiple of the one below it, the denominations form a 'canonical' system where simple greed is provably optimal: repeatedly take as many of the largest coin as fit, then move down. Since the smallest coin is 1, every target is reachable.

name: First Prefix Pair
background: When one string is a prefix of another, sorting places them next to each other with the shorter one first. So scanning adjacent pairs in sorted order and asking whether the later string starts with the earlier one finds every such relationship.
task: Read N distinct strings, sort them lexicographically, and find the first adjacent pair where one string is a prefix of the other. Print the prefix string followed by the longer string, or NONE if no such pair exists.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated strings, all distinct.
constraints:
N: 2-100
strings: 1-20 lowercase letters, all distinct

4
car card dog cat
test1_input:
4
car card dog cat
test7_input:
6
q w e r t y
test12_input:
6
ba zz b ca ab abc

name: Least Similar Neighbours
background: After sorting, only adjacent pairs are examined, and each is measured by how many leading characters the two strings share before differing. This time the SMALLEST such length wins, marking the biggest jump in the sorted order. Ties go to the earliest pair.
task: Read N strings, sort them lexicographically, and find the adjacent pair with the shortest common prefix (earliest such pair on ties). Print the two strings followed by that common-prefix length.

Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated strings.

task: Read N words and print all distinct words sorted by decreasing frequency, breaking ties by placing the lexicographically smaller word first.

name: Top Selling Product
background: Every product ID is counted and the highest count wins. When several products tie at the top, the smallest numeric ID among them is chosen, so the tie-break is by value rather than by order of appearance.
task: Read N product sale IDs and print the ID that appears most often. If several tie, print the smallest numeric ID among them.

Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

task: Read N tile colours and print each distinct colour once, sorted from most frequent to least, breaking ties by which colour appears earlier in the input.

name: XOR Over a Range
background: XOR compares numbers bit by bit and keeps a 1 wherever exactly one side had a 1. Its key property is that XORing a value twice cancels it out, so a running prefix of XORs can answer any range by XORing the prefix at the range end with the prefix just before the start.
task: Read an array A of N non-negative integers and Q queries. For each query (l, r) print the XOR of A[l] through A[r] inclusive, one answer per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.
Next Q lines: l and r, separated by a space.

name: XOR of Bitmasks Over a Range
background: Each value is a bitmask, and XORing masks together records which bits were flipped an odd number of times. Because XORing the same mask twice cancels it, a prefix of running XORs lets any range be answered with a single XOR of two prefixes.
task: Read a sequence S of N bitmasks and Q inclusive queries. For each query (l, r) print the parity mask obtained by XORing all S[i] for i in [l, r], as a non-negative integer, one per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.
Next Q lines: l and r, separated by a space.

name: Odd Toggle Check
background: Each lamp records 0 or 1 for whether it was toggled. XORing a range of these bits gives 1 exactly when an ODD number of toggles happened in that range, since pairs of toggles cancel. A prefix of running XORs answers any range instantly.
task: Read N toggle records T[i] in {0, 1} and Q queries. For each query (l, r) print 1 if the XOR of T[l..r] is 1 (an odd number of toggles), otherwise 0, one answer per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated bits, each 0 or 1.
Next Q lines: l and r, separated by a space.
constraints:
N, Q: 1-50
1 <= l <= r <= N
bits: 0 or 1

name: XOR of Transaction IDs
background: XOR is its own inverse: applying the same value twice returns you to where you started. That means a running prefix of XORs over the log can answer any inclusive range by combining just two stored prefixes.
task: Read a log of N non-negative transaction identifiers and Q reports. For each report (l, r) print the XOR of all identifiers in the inclusive range, one answer per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.
Next Q lines: l and r, separated by a space.
constraints:
N, Q: 1-50
1 <= l <= r <= N
identifiers: 0-1000000

name: Masked XOR Over a Range
background: Each query carries an extra mask that is XORed into the result alongside the range. Since XOR is associative and order does not matter, the mask can simply be combined with the range XOR at the end. A prefix of running XORs handles the range part.
task: Read an array V of N integers and Q queries, each giving l, r and a mask m. For each query print m XOR V[l] XOR ... XOR V[r], one answer per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N, Q (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.
Next Q lines: l, r and m, separated by spaces.
constraints:
N, Q: 1-50
1 <= l <= r <= N
values and masks: 0-1000000

name: Is P a Subsequence
background: A subsequence keeps the original order but allows gaps, so 'ace' is a subsequence of 'abcde' even though those letters are not adjacent. This differs from a substring, which must be contiguous. A greedy left-to-right scan taking the earliest possible match always works.
task: Read two strings P and T. Print YES if P appears as a subsequence of T (same order, gaps allowed), otherwise NO.
input_format:
Line 1: the string P.
Line 2: the string T.
constraints:
length of P and T: 1-100
both strings contain lowercase letters only

abcde

abcde

aabbcc

bccccc

background: The command pattern must be readable from the log in order, with gaps allowed. Scanning the log left to right and grabbing each needed character at the earliest opportunity always succeeds if any match exists, and it produces the earliest possible positions.
task: Read a command pattern C and a robot log L. If C can be read from L as a subsequence, print the 1-based positions in L of each matched command, taking the earliest possible match. Otherwise print -1.

Line 2: the string L.
constraints:
length of C and L: 1-100
both strings contain lowercase letters only

name: Where the Pattern Finishes
background: The pattern must appear inside the source in order but not necessarily consecutively. Matching greedily from the left takes each element at the earliest chance, which also makes the final matched position as early as possible. Positions start at 1, leaving 0 to mean 'no match'.
task: Read a pattern sequence A and a source sequence B. If A occurs as a subsequence of B, print the 1-based index in B of the last matched element under earliest-possible matching. Otherwise print 0.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers (pattern A).
Line 3: M.
Line 4: M space-separated integers (source B).

name: Where the Motif Starts
background: The motif must appear in order within the genome, with gaps allowed. Greedy matching from the left grabs each base at the earliest opportunity, which yields the earliest possible starting position for a complete match. If the motif cannot be matched at all, -1 is reported.
task: Read a DNA motif P and a genomic string G. If P is a subsequence of G, print the smallest 1-based index in G where the first character of a valid match occurs. Otherwise print -1.

name: Is B a Rotation of A
background: A cyclic rotation shifts every character around a circle, so 'cdab' is a rotation of 'abcd'. A neat trick: B is a rotation of A exactly when B appears somewhere inside A joined to itself, since that doubled string contains every rotation as a contiguous stretch.
task: Read two equal-length lowercase strings A and B. Print YES if B is a cyclic rotation of A, otherwise NO.
input_format:

Line 2: the string B.
constraints:
length of A and B: 1-100, always equal
both strings contain lowercase letters only

name: Dial Rotation Check
background: A cyclic shift moves every entry the same number of steps around the dial, with entries falling off one end reappearing at the other. Checking every possible shift amount is enough, since there are only as many rotations as there are positions.
task: Read two equal-length arrays of digits representing circular dial positions. Print True if the second is a cyclic shift of the first, otherwise False.

name: Conveyor Layout Check
background: The conveyor loops around, so a layout observed later may simply be the same layout shifted by some number of positions. Testing every possible shift amount decides whether the two observations differ only by such a cyclic shift.
task: Read two equal-length sequences of tokens representing a conveyor's circular layout at two times. Print yes if one is a cyclic shift of the other, otherwise no.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.
Line 3: M.
Line 4: M space-separated integers.

name: Largest Rectangle in the Histogram
background: A rectangle is drawn across a contiguous run of bars, and its height is limited by the SHORTEST bar in that run, since the rectangle must fit under all of them. Its area is that shortest height times the number of bars. Widening a run can only lower or keep the limiting height.
task: Read N bar heights and print the maximum area of any rectangle formed by contiguous bars, where area is the number of bars times the minimum height among them.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.

name: Largest Rectangle Through a Bar
background: Every rectangle considered must cover bar K, so the chosen run has to start at or before K and end at or after it. As before the rectangle's height is capped by the shortest bar in the run. Bar indices start at 0.
task: Read N bar heights and an index K. Print the largest area of any contiguous rectangle that includes bar K, where area is the width times the minimum height in the chosen run.
input_format:
Line 1: N, K (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.
constraints:
N: 1-100
K: 0 to N-1, indices are 0-based
heights: 0-10000

name: Best Block of Fixed Width
background: The width is fixed at W bars, so only the placement of the block can change. Each block's height is capped by its shortest bar, and the area is that height times W. The goal is the placement giving the largest area.
task: Read N bar heights and a width W. Print the maximum area of any contiguous block of exactly W bars, where area is W times the minimum height in that block.
input_format:
Line 1: N, W (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.

name: Count Tall-Enough Segments
background: A contiguous segment qualifies when EVERY bar in it reaches at least T, which is the same as saying its minimum height is at least T. The bound is inclusive, so a bar of exactly height T is fine. Single-bar segments count too.
task: Read N bar heights and a threshold T. Print how many contiguous segments have a minimum height of at least T.
input_format:
Line 1: N, T (space-separated).
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.

name: Best Rectangle for Each Bar
background: For each bar in turn, the rectangle is stretched as far left and right as possible while every bar it covers stays at least as tall as the chosen bar. That makes the chosen bar the limiting height, and the area is its height times the resulting width.
task: Read N bar heights. For each bar i, print the maximum area of a contiguous rectangle in which bar i is the limiting (minimum-height) bar, computed as the width times h[i]. Print the N values in order.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers.

name: Smallest Missing Tag
background: Only the window from 0 to N matters; any value outside it is ignored entirely, as are repeats. Because there are N+1 candidate labels but only N entries, at least one label in that window is always missing, so an answer always exists.
task: Read N integer tags and print the smallest non-negative integer in the range 0 to N that does not appear among them. Values outside 0..N are ignored.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Smallest Free Seat
background: Seats are numbered from 1, and only the window 1 to N+1 is considered; anything outside it, along with repeats, is ignored. Since that window holds N+1 candidates but only N entries were reported, a free seat always exists.
task: Read N occupied seat numbers and print the smallest seat label in the range 1 to N+1 that is unoccupied. Values outside that range are ignored.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Smallest Free Product Code
background: Codes begin at 1000, and only the window from 1000 to 1000+N is considered; anything outside it, along with repeats, is ignored. That window holds N+1 candidates while only N codes were reported, so a free code always exists.
task: Read N reported product codes and print the smallest code in the inclusive range 1000 to 1000+N that does not occur. Codes outside that range are ignored.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Smallest Missing Firmware Version
background: Versions start at 0, and only the window 0 to N is considered; duplicates and out-of-range values are ignored. With N+1 candidate versions and only N reported entries, some version in the window is always absent.
task: Read N reported firmware versions and print the smallest non-negative version in the range 0 to N that is not present. Duplicates and values outside 0..N are ignored.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Smallest Free Badge ID
background: Badge IDs start at 1, and only the window 1 to N+1 is searched; repeats and out-of-range values are ignored. Since that window contains N+1 candidates and only N badges were assigned, at least one ID is always available.
task: Read N assigned badge IDs and print the smallest available ID within the range 1 to N+1 that does not appear. Values outside that range are ignored.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Evaluate Postfix Arithmetic
background: In postfix notation the operator comes AFTER its two operands, so '3 4 +' means 3 plus 4. Numbers are pushed onto a stack and each operator pops two values, applies itself and pushes the result. Order matters for subtraction and division: the value pushed first is the left operand. Division truncates toward zero, so -7 divided by 2 gives -3.
task: Read a valid postfix expression of signed integers and the binary operators + - * / (division truncates toward zero). Print the single integer left on the stack.
input_format: Line 1: the whitespace-delimited postfix expression.
constraints:
tokens: 1-50
operand values: -10000 to 10000
division by zero never occurs

name: Evaluate Postfix Booleans
background: Postfix places the operator after its operands, so 'T F AND' means T combined with F using AND. AND yields true only when both operands are true; OR yields true when at least one is. Values are pushed onto a stack and each operator pops two and pushes its result.
task: Read a postfix stream of the tokens T and F with the binary operators AND and OR. Print the final value as T or F.
input_format: Line 1: the whitespace-delimited postfix stream.
constraints:
tokens: 1-50
operand tokens are T or F
sample_input: T F AND T OR
test1_input: T F AND T OR
test7_input: F F OR F OR F OR
test8_input: T T AND T AND T AND
test10_input: F T OR F AND T OR T AND
test11_input: F F AND F AND T AND T AND T OR T OR
test12_input: T F OR T OR

name: Evaluate Postfix with Modulo
background: Postfix puts the operator after its operands, and each operator pops two values with the earlier-pushed one acting as the left operand. The modulo here takes the sign of the DIVIDEND, so -7 mod 3 gives -1 rather than 2. This matches the remainder left by division that truncates toward zero.
task: Read a valid postfix program of signed integers and the binary operators + - * % (the remainder takes the sign of the dividend). Print the single integer result.
input_format: Line 1: the whitespace-delimited postfix program.
constraints:
tokens: 1-50
operand values: -10000 to 10000
modulo by zero never occurs

name: Evaluate Postfix Max and Min
background: Postfix places each operator after the two values it works on. Here 'max' pops two shipment sizes and pushes the larger, while 'min' pushes the smaller. Since both operations are symmetric, the order of the two operands does not affect the result.
task: Read a postfix sequence of non-negative integers and the binary operators max and min. Print the final integer remaining.
input_format: Line 1: the whitespace-delimited postfix sequence.
sample_input: 3 9 max 5 min
test1_input: 3 9 max 5 min
test7_input: 1000000 0 min 7 max
test12_input: 17 22 max 3 max 5 min 24 max 7 min 19 max

name: Evaluate Postfix with Comparison
background: Postfix places the operator after its operands. The '>' operator pops two values, treating the one pushed FIRST as the left side, and pushes 1 if that left side is strictly greater than the right, otherwise 0. The result is an ordinary number that later operators can use.
task: Read a valid postfix expression of signed integers using the binary operators + and >, where '>' pops b then a and pushes 1 if a > b else 0. Print the single final integer.
input_format: Line 1: the whitespace-delimited postfix expression.

name: Merge Touching Meetings
background: Sorting the bookings by start time means each one only ever needs comparing against the block currently being built. Since intervals are closed and touching counts as merging, a booking joins the current block whenever its start is at most the block's current end.
task: Read N meeting bookings as closed intervals [start, end], where touching intervals merge. Print the minimal list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start, one 'start end' per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next N lines: start and end, separated by a space.
constraints:
N: 1-50
intervals satisfy start <= end
times: 0-100000

name: Consolidate IP Ranges
background: These ranges hold whole integers, so two ranges are ADJACENT when one ends exactly where the next begins minus one, leaving no gap between them. Adjacent ranges merge just like overlapping ones, which means the merge test allows a start one past the current end.
task: Read N IP ranges as inclusive integer intervals [L, R], where adjacent ranges (R+1 equals the next L) also merge. Print the sorted list of merged ranges, one 'L R' per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next N lines: L and R, separated by a space.
constraints:
N: 1-50
intervals satisfy L <= R
values: 0-100000

name: Union of Half-Open Windows
background: Half-open windows [start, end) exclude their end, so a window ending at 10 and one starting at 10 share no time at all and stay separate. Only windows that genuinely overlap are merged, meaning the next start must be strictly less than the current end.
task: Read N sensor windows as half-open intervals [start, end), where touching windows are NOT merged. Print the minimal sorted list of non-overlapping half-open intervals, one per line.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next N lines: start and end, separated by a space.
constraints:
N: 1-50
intervals satisfy start < end
times: 0-100000

name: Total Covered Seat Length
background: Segments that overlap or merely touch are fused into one, so a point covered by several segments is still counted only once. After merging, each block contributes its own length, and those lengths are added up.
task: Read N seat segments as intervals [a, b] with one decimal place, where touching intervals merge. Print the total covered length after merging, with one decimal place.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next N lines: a and b as decimals, separated by a space.
constraints:
N: 1-50
intervals satisfy a <= b
values: 0.0-1000.0, given with one decimal place

name: Count Disjoint Coverage Blocks
background: Segments merge only when they genuinely overlap; segments that merely touch at a single endpoint stay separate, so the merge test requires the next start to be strictly less than the current end. The answer counts how many separate blocks survive.
task: Read N coverage segments as intervals [s, e], where touching endpoints do NOT merge. Print the number of disjoint segments remaining after merging genuine overlaps.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next N lines: s and e, separated by a space.
constraints:
N: 1-50
intervals satisfy s <= e
values: 0-100000

name: Pattern Fits the Words
background: A bijection pairs each pattern letter with exactly one word AND each word with exactly one letter, so no two letters may share a word and no word may serve two letters. The pattern and the word sequence must also be the same length. 'abba' fits 'dog cat cat dog' but not 'dog dog dog dog'.
task: Read a pattern string of letters and a sequence of words. Print YES if each letter can be mapped one-to-one to a distinct word so the pattern reproduces the sequence, otherwise NO.

name: Template Expands to Data
background: Each placeholder must always expand to the same token, and no two different placeholders may expand to the same token. Both conditions together make the correspondence a bijection. The template and the data line must also hold the same number of tokens.
task: Read a template of placeholders and a data line of tokens. Print 1 if an exact one-to-one mapping between placeholders and tokens makes the template expand to the data, otherwise 0.
input_format:
Line 1: space-separated placeholders.
Line 2: space-separated data tokens.
constraints:
each line has 1-50 tokens
tokens: 1-20 characters, no spaces

cat dog cat

name: Symbols Match Items
background: Each symbol must map to exactly one item and each item back to exactly one symbol, checked at every position. A single position where a symbol reuses a different item, or where two symbols share an item, breaks the match.
task: Read a pattern of digit symbols and a list of item names. Print MATCH if each symbol maps to exactly one item and each item to exactly one symbol across all positions, otherwise NO MATCH.
input_format:
Line 1: space-separated digit symbols.
Line 2: space-separated item names.
constraints:
each line has 1-50 tokens
item names: 1-20 characters, no spaces

1 2 1 3
apple pear apple plum

apple pear apple plum
test7_input:

name: Tags Map to Log Fields
background: The correspondence must be bidirectional: a tag always pairs with the same field, and a field is never claimed by two different tags. Both sequences must also be the same length for a position-by-position mapping to exist at all.
task: Read a sequence of tag tokens and a sequence of log-field tokens. Print true if a bidirectional one-to-one mapping from tags to fields matches every position, otherwise false.
input_format:

name: Closest Two Values
background: Sorting the values first means the two closest ones must end up next to each other, so only neighbouring pairs in the sorted order need checking rather than every possible pair. Duplicate values give a gap of 0, which is the smallest possible.
task: Read N integers and print the minimum absolute difference between any two of them.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Indices of the Closest Timestamps
background: The two timestamps with the smallest gap are wanted, but the ORIGINAL positions must be reported, not their positions after any sorting. Where several pairs tie at the same smallest gap, the pair with the smallest first index wins, then the smallest second.
task: Read N timestamps and find two distinct ones with the smallest absolute gap. Print their original 1-based indices (smaller index first), breaking ties by smallest first index then smallest second.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: The Two Closest Scores
background: Two different players whose scores are nearest to each other are wanted, and it is their SCORES that get printed rather than their positions. The two scores are printed in nondecreasing order, so the smaller comes first.
task: Read N player scores and find two different players whose scores differ least. Print the two scores in nondecreasing order. If several pairs tie, use the pair with the smallest first index then smallest second.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Closest Gap and How Often
background: First the smallest gap between any two elements is found, then every unordered pair achieving exactly that gap is counted. Repeated values push the smallest gap to 0 and can create many qualifying pairs at once.
task: Read N integers and print two values: the minimum absolute difference between any pair, and the number of unordered pairs achieving that minimum.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Earliest Closest Pair
background: Among all pairs of positions with i less than j, the one whose values are nearest is wanted. When several pairs share that smallest difference, the answer is the lexicographically smallest index pair, meaning the smallest i, and among those the smallest j.
task: Read N integers and find the pair of indices (i < j) whose values differ least. If several pairs tie, print the lexicographically smallest index pair. Print the two 1-based indices.
input_format:
Line 1: N.
Line 2: N space-separated integers.

name: Text Editor with Undo
background: The typed characters form a stack: each TYPE pushes a character on top, and each UNDO removes whatever is currently on top. An UNDO with nothing to remove simply does nothing. What survives is read from oldest to newest.
task: Read N editor commands, each either 'TYPE c' (append character c) or 'UNDO' (remove the most recently appended character still present). Print the final text, or an empty line if no text remains.
input_format:

Next N lines: either 'TYPE c' or 'UNDO'.
